summary: A speaker at the end of a long fight gives both sides a share of the blame and claims no credit for the outcome.
realLife: Lincoln's second inaugural, March 4, 1865, said neither side expected the war's size, both prayed to the same God, and the cause was an offense carried by North and South alike. He took no victory lap and closed with one long sentence about binding wounds.
sources: Read the whole address on the Presidency Project page and noted who is blamed, whether credit is claimed, and the sentence shapes.
inGame: The `stand` and `close` sections of the speech planner, pulled by humble and by who held the office during the trouble.

turns.what: The winner puts all the blame on the other side and takes the credit.
turns.writesBack: The stand section names the other side as the cause; the close claims the win.

turns.what: The speaker names the cause but spreads blame only to the speaker's own side.
turns.pulledBy: a world fact: the speaker's party ran the place during the trouble
turns.writesBack: The speech records an admission with no peace offer.
